clue.text: Working class under this perhaps even better?

parts.note: even means level or flat, as a surface
to better a score is to cap it, outdoing it

explanation.surface: A wry question whether the working class might be even better off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' reads as an adjective but is the verb: to cap something is to better it. The flat cap is the cloth cap stereotypically worn by British working-class men.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth cap is the headgear traditionally linked with British working men, so they are found under one.

clue.text: Endlessly lie when taking care of failure

indicators.note: endlessly says the word for a lie loses its final letter

parts.note: a fib is a small lie
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
c/o is the postal abbreviation for care of

explanation.surface: Someone keeps lying while looking after things and it ends in failure.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiasco is a complete and humiliating failure, a synonym.

clue.text: Part of hoof upset horse?

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means the word is turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lamina is one of the thin layers inside a horse's hoof

explanation.surface: A puzzle over what part of a hoof could upset a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse is an example of a beast, hence the question mark marking a definition by example.

clue.text: See, audience judges work here?

parts.note: to see someone is to date them, and courting is an old word for dating
a theatre's audience is the house, as in 'a full house'

explanation.surface: Pointing out to an audience the place where judges do their work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an exclamation calling attention, but it is the verb to see, meaning to go out with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Trials are heard by judges in a building set aside for law courts.

clue.text: Head, essentially dirty old man

parts.note: the pate is the top of the head

indicators.note: essentially points to the essence, the central letter of the word dirty

explanation.surface: Calling the boss, at heart, a dirty old man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dirty old man' is a set phrase, but 'dirty' only gives its middle letter. Albert Steptoe, of the BBC sitcom 'Steptoe and Son', was known as a dirty old man.
explanation.definitionFit: Pater is the old public-school Latin word for father, and 'old man' is slang for one's dad.

clue.text: Bad egg, Albert partially retired and scrounged

indicators.note: retired says the hidden letters are read backwards
partially says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Albert, a bad egg who has given up work, lives by cadging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns the run DEGGALB, inside 'Bad egg, Albert', backwards. Albert is old Steptoe, the scrounging father in the sitcom 'Steptoe and Son'.
explanation.definitionFit: To blag is British slang for getting something free by talking one's way into it, much like cadging.

clue.text: See man, mostly well off

parts.note: a bishop is one of the men, the pieces, in chess

indicators.note: mostly says the word for well off loses its last letter

parts.note: someone well off is rich

explanation.surface: Telling someone to look at a fellow who is quite comfortably off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to look, but it is the noun: a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the district a bishop governs, which is also called his bishopric.

clue.text: While touring album peaks

indicators.note: touring means going round, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: as can mean while, as in 'as we spoke'
an LP is a long-playing record album

explanation.surface: A band visits the mountains while on tour promoting an album.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the great mountain range of Europe, famous for their peaks.

clue.text: Lots of prospects after this good antique career?

parts.note: something antique is old
to career is to rush along headlong

explanation.surface: Wondering whether dealing in old antiques makes a good career with prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prospects' are not job chances but people prospecting for gold, and 'career' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In a stampede for newly found gold, many prospectors arrive to stake claims.

clue.text: Files a bit around foot

indicators.note: around means the phrase 'a bit' is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a tad is a little bit
the foot of something is its base

explanation.surface: Some papers lying a little way around the bottom of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A database is an organised collection of computer records or files.

clue.text: I'm going to pass on gold frames

indicators.note: frames means surrounds, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
to pass on is a euphemism for to die

explanation.surface: A dying person bequeathing gold picture frames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pass on' looks like handing something down, but it means to die.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a French farewell said by someone departing, like 'goodbye'.

clue.text: One takes off with paper — good things for sale

parts.note: an exam paper is a test
pi, short for pious, means good
a lot is an item or batch offered at auction

explanation.surface: Someone leaves with a newspaper and some bargains on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: PI for pious, meaning good, is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies new aircraft, so taking off is a routine part of the job.

clue.text: Harry H Corbett: a cross windbag

indicators.note: to harry is to harass, so these letters are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: Calling the actor Harry H Corbett a bad-tempered talker.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry H Corbett played Harold in 'Steptoe and Son'; here his first name is the anagram signal and the cross is X, not a temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A windbag talks endlessly and emptily, just like a constant prattler.

clue.text: Rag and Bone

definitions.meaning: to rag someone is to tease them
one of the curved bones of the chest

explanation.surface: A rag-and-bone man, the scrap dealer of 'Steptoe and Son'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib someone is to tease them, and ribs are the curved bones of the chest.

clue.text: One calling out "help" on programme after turning over film

indicators.note: turning over means the film's title is read backwards

parts.note: ET is the Spielberg film about an alien

indicators.note: out means the letters of the cry for help are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written
ER is the American hospital drama series

explanation.surface: Someone shouting for help on a TV show after seeing a film upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning over' reverses ET; 'out' mixes the letters of HELP into LEPH, so 'calling out' is not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rings another person up is making a call on the phone.

clue.text: Moving girl, Steptoe and Son: they might move furniture?

indicators.note: moving says the letters of these words shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Steptoe and Son, removal men with a girl, shifting furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son ran a rag-and-bone business in the BBC sitcom.
explanation.definitionFit: Poltergeists are noisy spirits said to throw objects and shift furniture about.

clue.text: "Sort rubbish? We must go outside" — put down characters without script?

parts.note: a type is a sort or kind

indicators.note: must go outside says these letters wrap around the other piece

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A house rule about sorting the rubbish and taking it outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' are letters, and 'without script' contrasts typed text with handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Using a typewriter puts letters on the page by machine rather than in handwriting.

clue.text: Rests back in a bed and let oneself down

indicators.note: in says the reversed word sits inside the others
back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: someone resting lies down

explanation.surface: Someone lying back in bed feels they have failed themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let oneself down' reads as disappointing oneself, but it means descending by rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Abseiling is descending a cliff by a rope, lowering oneself down.

clue.text: Balconies tense? Royal Ascot meeting?

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the monarch
Royal Ascot is a famous horse-race meeting in England

explanation.surface: Tense spectators on the balconies at Royal Ascot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal Ascot' looks like one name, but Royal gives ER and Ascot meeting gives a set of horse races.
explanation.definitionFit: Terraces are tiers of seating or standing, like the raised galleries of a stand.

clue.text: Maybe watch here — dodgy back? Steptoe runs inside

indicators.note: inside says that letter goes within the rearranged words
dodgy means unsound, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Old Steptoe with a bad back is still running, watch in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' gives BEASTPOCKET, which 'inside' opens for R. 'watch' is the noun, a timepiece, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket watch may be carried in the chest pocket of a jacket.

clue.text: Concerning story, fellow gets help

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a story can be a lie

explanation.surface: A man telling a tale about himself is given assistance.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief is assistance given to those in need, such as aid.

clue.text: Determined, picking up bargain at end of day

indicators.note: picking up means hearing, so the word is given by its sound

parts.note: a bargain is a steal

indicators.note: at end of says to take the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A shopper resolved to pick up a bargain at the end of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A steely person has resolve as hard as steel, unyielding.

clue.text: Lug stuff that's no good

indicators.note: no good says the abbreviation for good is removed

parts.note: gear means kit or stuff

explanation.surface: Carrying stuff around that is useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lug' looks like a verb meaning to haul, but it is British slang for the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Lug, or lughole, is British slang for the organ of hearing.

clue.text: Wearing sweatshirt that's most black

indicators.note: wearing hints at the fabric being worn out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone in a sweatshirt that is the darkest of them all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' looks like putting on clothes but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Swarthy means dark-skinned or dark, so the superlative is darkest.

clue.text: Place again on TV

parts.note: re means on or about
a TV is a television set

explanation.surface: Putting something back on the television.
explanation.definitionFit: To reset is to set or position something once more, as with a bone.

clue.text: Woman's over leading actor

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A woman has got over the lead in the play.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero is the principal male character in a story or film, its lead.

clue.text: Hercules struggling to carry old Steptoe: like his attitude?

indicators.note: to carry says the rearranged letters hold the next piece
struggling says the hero's name is wrestled into a new letter order

explanation.surface: Hercules straining to lift old man Steptoe, questioning his outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert Steptoe, the father in 'Steptoe and Son', was the archetypal dirty old man.
explanation.definitionFit: A lustful, leering outlook was the old rag-and-bone man's trademark in the sitcom.

clue.text: Row over current smell

indicators.note: over means covering, so one piece sits over the other

parts.note: nose means a sense of smell
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An argument about a lingering odour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow here: a din, not a line or a boat trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A row is a loud racket or din, which is a sound.

clue.text: Arrange rubbish at front of carriage

indicators.note: at front of says the first piece comes before the second

parts.note: to rubbish someone is to diss them
carriage is bearing or posture, a pose

explanation.surface: Organising rubbish at the front of a train carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispose things is to set them out in order, a formal sense of arrange.

clue.text: Economical yard after the short argument

indicators.note: after says the yard piece comes after the others
short says the word the loses its final letter

parts.note: a rift is a falling-out

explanation.surface: A cheap yard sale following a brief quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrifty people are careful with money, sparing and frugal.
